title: Known-state and known-model controls temper synthetic latent-line false alarms
statement: In the same binary latent-line family, conditioning word shuffles on the true state rejects 0–3 of 30 null books across the tested settings, while the known-model posterior-predictive null rejects 0–3. Conditioning on four observed proxy words still rejects 19–30, whereas 16- or 32-word count proxies reject 0–4 in these trials; all methods reject all 30 examples of one strong planted transition. True states and the exact generator parameters are oracle information, and these small synthetic results do not validate a manuscript null.
check: Calibrate an estimated, rather than known, latent model on independent simulations and external texts, including misspecified state counts, nonbinary vocabularies, dependent endpoints, varying line lengths, missing data and page effects. Compare posterior predictive checks with exact-word conditional nulls, enforce movement and support gates, and quantify uncertainty over fitted parameters. Freeze the eight intended edge pairs and aggregate test before held-out evaluation; no null rejection should be interpreted as proof of direct transitions without establishing robustness to latent mixtures.
simulation: For each of 30 seeds, make six pages of 36 lines. Each line independently has a binary latent state. At each word, first and last bits independently equal that state with probability p (otherwise flip), so there is no direct cross-word dependence given the state. Use p=.7,.8,.9, and probe lengths 4, 16 and 32; leave eight subsequent words for seven equality-of-edge tests. An independent-word condition chooses both bits independently and uniformly. The positive alternative uses p=.8, but its target first bit copies the preceding target word’s last bit with probability .85. All methods use 39 simulated nulls and one-sided add-one p-values with threshold .05.
conditional_shuffle: Within each page and exact target position shuffle complete target words jointly across lines, stratifying either on the generator’s true latent bit (oracle) or on the count of ones in the last bits of the probe words. This preserves each complete-word multiset per cell and hence overlapping word boundaries; every shuffle asserts exact Counter equality. Refuse a replicate with fewer than 30 cells containing more than one word value; none of the reported cases was refused. Proxy majority error rates are measured using the hidden synthetic state and cannot be known for real manuscript lines. The latent-null and positive simulations reuse seed indices across settings and use only 30 books each.
posterior_predictive: The follow-up parametric null assumes the correct latent model, prior P(state=1)=1/2 and known p, and computes P(state=1 | probe) from the count of probe end bits. Independently sample a state from that posterior for each line, generate eight target words from the known conditionally independent emissions, and compare the same seven-edge count against 39 such samples. This integrates latent-state uncertainty and preserves shared words within each generated line; unlike the permutation, it does not preserve the exact observed word or edge marginals. The independent-word condition uses known p=.5. No model fitting, prior uncertainty or misspecification is included.
limitations: The true-state oracle and the known-model posterior predictive check use information unavailable in the manuscript. More probe words leave less text to test and count strata may become sparse on real folios. The simulation assumes binary symbols, stationary p and independent emissions; it does not cover mixed page rates, uncertain tokens, variable line lengths, genuine vocabulary or model misspecification. Thirty books and 39 null samples provide low-resolution uncertainty; zero to three rejections is not proof of nominal size. Parameter choices were exploratory follow-ups to prior results. The score is a surrogate equality statistic rather than the full eight-pair aggregate. No manuscript data were examined.
